steps.title: Initialize the fixed code lengths

quiz.prompt: Which values are stored in the fixed length vector?

choices.text: The number of code bits assigned to each symbol.

hints.text: Write one byte per length, indexed by symbol.
Do not remove reserved fixed symbols from the table definition.

steps.title: Clear one table before counting

quiz.prompt: Why clear the table on every build?

choices.text: Counts belong to the new alphabet, not its predecessor.
The source vector is always a string.
A cleared count automatically gives every symbol a code.

hints.text: Clear count words rather than the read-only format tables.
Retain separate cursors for input lengths and output counts.

steps.title: Count lengths without treating zero as a code

quiz.prompt: Does a zero length denote a zero-bit data code?

choices.text: Yes, one that produces a zero byte.

hints.text: Validate before multiplying a length into a word offset.
Track declared slots and present symbols separately.

steps.title: Compute placement offsets and prefix space

quiz.prompt: What does placement offset 24 for length eight mean?

choices.text: The input cursor is at byte 24.
Twenty-four present symbols have shorter codes.
Every eight-bit code has numerical value 24.

hints.text: An exclusive offset is measured before adding this length’s count.
Use a separate signed prefix-space calculation to detect oversubscription.

steps.title: Apply the permitted sparse-alphabet cases

quiz.prompt: Which incomplete data-alphabet case is permitted here?

choices.text: Any alphabet whose lengths are at most fifteen.
A single present symbol with length one.

hints.text: Keep strict code-length policy separate from data policies.
An unused distance alphabet is different from an unused bit pattern in a one-code alphabet.

steps.title: Place symbols in length and numerical order

quiz.prompt: Where is fixed literal zero in the ordered array?

hints.text: Enumerating symbols upward supplies the tie-break order within a length.
Store symbol IDs as halfwords, not length bytes.

steps.title: Start a symbol search at the shortest length

quiz.prompt: Which state survives between symbol calls?

hints.text: Reset code-search variables without discarding unread input bits.
Count zero is not a search length.

steps.title: Reuse buffered bits or refill one byte

quiz.prompt: When should a symbol search discard the remaining header-byte bits?

choices.text: It should retain them and consume them in sequence.

hints.text: Check the available count before a byte load.
Use the same compressed end bound as the ordinary bit reader.

steps.title: Compare a code in arrival order

quiz.prompt: What identifies a matching code at one length?

choices.text: Its difference from the first code lies within that length’s count.
Its numerical value equals the symbol number.

hints.text: Huffman code order differs from an ordinary low-bit numerical field.
Advance code length only after testing this length’s range.

steps.title: Look up the selected symbol ID

quiz.prompt: Does every value returned by this helper represent a row byte?

choices.text: No; the selected alphabet and caller determine its meaning.
Only if the source address is aligned.

hints.text: Keep the within-length rank separate from the final symbol ID.
Use the array after the count words, not the count cursor itself.

steps.title: Separate literals, end-of-block and lengths

quiz.prompt: What does symbol 256 do?

choices.text: Ends this block and follows its completion path.

hints.text: Classify before interpreting extra-bit tables.
Keep end-of-block separate from the retained final-block flag.

steps.title: Emit one literal within the row window

quiz.prompt: What bounds a literal store?

choices.text: The current output cursor must precede its expected end.
The compressed cursor must equal the checksum address.
The symbol must contain eight code bits.

hints.text: A literal’s code length and its one-byte output size are different quantities.
Reuse the existing exact-output check after the block ends.

steps.title: Expand a length code and its extra bits

quiz.prompt: What is the reconstructed length in this fixture?

hints.text: Validate the symbol before turning it into a table index.
Preserve the base across a helper that returns through the same result register.

steps.title: Decode the separate distance alphabet

quiz.prompt: What does distance symbol zero select?

choices.text: The first distance-table entry, whose base is one.

hints.text: Use the distance table rather than decoding through the literal/length table.
Bound reserved symbols before either lookup.

steps.title: Construct the full backward distance

quiz.prompt: May a zero-extra-bit distance fetch a new input byte?

choices.text: Yes, every distance consumes a byte.
No; the zero-bit read retains the input cursor.

hints.text: A table symbol and its reconstructed distance are distinct values.
The ordinary zero-bit field returns zero without consuming input.

steps.title: Admit a match before deriving copy addresses

quiz.prompt: Which history bound is needed in addition to the advertised window?

choices.text: Distance must fit bytes actually produced.
Distance must equal the current source-file offset.
Distance must divide the row width.

hints.text: Check counts before subtracting a backward pointer.
A large window does not create earlier output bytes.

steps.title: Copy forward through overlapping history

quiz.prompt: Where does the second match byte come from here?

choices.text: The output byte produced by the first match iteration.

hints.text: Overlapping matches depend on newly produced bytes.
Keep compressed-input and history-copy cursors separate.

steps.title: Read the three dynamic description counts

quiz.prompt: What does the first decoded count describe?

hints.text: These three fields use ordinary low-bit numerical reads.
Keep declared counts distinct from symbol-use restrictions.

steps.title: Clear all nineteen possible code-length entries

quiz.prompt: Why clear nineteen entries when only eighteen follow?

choices.text: The untransmitted symbol must remain absent.
The nineteenth entry is always a pixel byte.
The input requires an extra padding length.

hints.text: Reset absent entries before reading the advertised subset.
Block-local mutable lengths must not inherit an earlier alphabet.

steps.title: Place the three-bit lengths by their permutation

quiz.prompt: Where is the first received length stored?

choices.text: At the slot for code-length symbol sixteen.

hints.text: Use incoming position to index the order table, then use that symbol to index lengths.
The three-bit value is a length, not a symbol ID.

steps.title: Build the alphabet that describes the data alphabets

quiz.prompt: What does this intermediate Huffman table decode?

choices.text: Lengths and repeat operators for the two data alphabets.

hints.text: Use strict policy for the code-length alphabet.
Set one bounded combined range for both data alphabets.

steps.title: Distinguish a direct length from a repeat operator

quiz.prompt: What does decoded symbol one mean in this table?

choices.text: One code length whose value is one.

hints.text: The selected table determines the meaning of a decoded symbol.
Prepare a value and count; leave the bounded store to the shared region.

steps.title: Bound each expansion before storing its bytes

quiz.prompt: Which boundary limits a repeat expansion?

choices.text: The first alphabet boundary even when more declared entries remain.
The end of the declared combined length vector.

hints.text: Compare the run count before adding or storing.
Use one expansion loop for direct values and repeats.

steps.title: Repeat a previous length only when one exists

quiz.prompt: Can operation sixteen repeat a previous zero length?

choices.text: Yes, when a previous expanded entry exists.
No, it can repeat only nonzero lengths.

hints.text: Test predecessor existence before loading cursor minus one.
Preserve the repeated value across the extra-bit read.

steps.title: Expand a short run of zero lengths

quiz.prompt: What is the largest run produced by operation seventeen?

hints.text: Add the prescribed bias after reading the field.

steps.title: Expand a long run without bypassing the same bound

quiz.prompt: What does a run of 138 zeros populate?

hints.text: Code-length runs describe metadata rather than decoded image samples.
Reuse the existing expansion bound instead of a second unchecked loop.

steps.title: Require end-of-block before building the data tables

quiz.prompt: Why require a code for symbol 256?

choices.text: Every compressed block needs an end-of-block symbol.

hints.text: Check the literal/length portion rather than a distance entry.
